commands.speak: To understand why a nerve injury can numb a whole limb, look at the one cell that carries the signal.
These branches are dendrites, the listening end, gathering signals from thousands of other neurons at once.
They converge on the cell body, the soma, with the nucleus that keeps the cell alive.
The soma sums those inputs, and past a threshold it fires, all or nothing, never halfway.
The firing runs out along the axon, the output cable, which in a motor neuron stretches from your spine to your toe as a single cell nearly a metre long.
Fatty myelin wraps it in sleeves, and the bare gaps between them are the nodes of Ranvier.
Current cannot leak through myelin, so the signal leaps node to node, and that skipping is why these fibres carry impulses at over a hundred metres a second.
That leaping wave is the action potential, and it runs one way only: dendrites in, terminals out.
At the far end the axon splits into terminals, each ending in a small swelling.
Here the electrical story turns chemical: neurotransmitter is released across a tiny gap to the next cell.
Nothing touches, so the message is thrown across, and that gap is where nearly every drug acting on the brain does its work.
Four jobs in one cell: dendrites listen, the soma decides, the axon carries, the synapse hands it on.
